Cyprian of Carthage
SIP-ree-an
proper noun
From the Latin Cyprianus, “of Cyprus,” the name of the bishop of Carthage who was martyred under Valerian, c.200–258 AD.

See also: Cyprian of Carthage

📖 Biblical Definition

Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, called Cyprian of Carthage, was bishop of that great African city in the middle of the third century, and a leader of the Western church in a day of fierce persecution. Converted in mature years out of a life of rhetoric and worldly honour, he gave himself wholly to Christ, and as a shepherd he laboured to guide the flock through the storms of the Decian and Valerian persecutions, when many fell away under torture and the church wrestled how to receive the lapsed who repented. Cyprian counselled mercy joined to discipline, that the penitent be restored in order and not lightly. At the last he was himself called to the crown he had urged on others: under Valerian he was beheaded for the name of Christ in the year 258, and so was found faithful unto death. The dictionary honours Cyprian for his courage, his pastoral discipline, and his martyrdom, for the Lord saith, Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life (Rev 2:10). He counted not his life dear, that he might finish his course with joy, and the ministry which he had received of the Lord Jesus (Act 20:24). His blood, like that of the early witnesses, watered the church; and his steadfastness under the sword stands as a true testimony of the grace that upholds the saints in the day of trial, to whom it is given not only to believe, but also to suffer for Christ’s sake (Phi 1:29).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The bishop of Carthage, martyred under Valerian, honoured for his courage and pastoral discipline.

CYPRIAN OF CARTHAGE, bishop of Carthage in the third century.

He was converted in mature years and gave himself wholly to Christ.

He guided the church through the Decian and Valerian persecutions.

He was beheaded for the name of Christ under Valerian in 258.

His sacerdotal view of the church Rome later built upon.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A courageous martyr-bishop, yet whose sacerdotal episcopate and “no salvation outside the church” formula Rome later built upon.

expand to see more

Cyprian is honoured for his courage, his pastoral care of a flock under persecution, and his martyrdom under Valerian; the dictionary records what is honourable in him, that he was faithful unto death and sealed his witness with his blood.

Yet his error must be named. Cyprian taught a sacerdotal view of the episcopate, making the bishop a priest in succession and the visible church, bound to that office, the one ark of salvation. From him comes the formula extra ecclesiam nulla salus, “no salvation outside the church,” understood of the visible, episcopal church; and from him the saying that he cannot have God for his Father who hath not the church for his mother. Upon this Rome later built her whole structure of priestly mediation and papal claim. But Scripture knows no priesthood set between Christ and the believer save the one High Priest, the Lord Jesus, and the royal priesthood of all the saints (1Pe 2:9). The true church is the company of the elect, known to God, and salvation is found in Christ alone by faith, not in submission to a visible hierarchy. Cyprian’s sacerdotalism confounded the sign with the thing signified, and the dictionary names it as the seed of the sacramental and papal corruptions the Reformation called the church away from.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin for “of Cyprus,” Cyprian names the martyr-bishop of Carthage.

Cyprian of Carthage — Latin Cyprianus, “of Cyprus.”

He was bishop of Carthage, c.200–258 AD.

He guided the church through fierce persecution.

He was martyred under Valerian in the year 258.

His sacerdotal episcopate and “no salvation outside the church” Rome built upon.
